title: Russell Brand accusers 'haunted' for years by alleged crimes, court hears
description: Some of the women in Russell Brand's rape and sexual assault case have been "haunted" for years by what they allege he did to them, jurors have been t
body: Some of the women in Russell Brand's rape and sexual assault case have been "haunted" for years by what they allege he did to them, jurors have been told.In her closing speech at London's Southwark Crown Court on Friday, prosecutor Reil Karmy-Jones KC said the women had "nothing to gain" from coming forward apart from "some closure".Speaking for the defence, Polly Dyer told jurors Brand had pleaded guilty and been fined over possession of cannabis in 1995, but had no other "convictions, cautions, reprimands or warnings". Brand, 51, is on trial facing seven charges; three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one allegation of attempted indecent assault. He denies the charges.Karmy-Jones KC told the court that this case brings together six different women, none of whom knows each other.She said that while all the alleged victims have since moved on with their lives, due to this trial they have been forced to "relive what has happened to them".None of the women involved has "sought the limelight" or "any kind of publicity", she said, adding there was "no benefit to them from perhaps some closure."Referring to Brand's accuser's evidence the prosecutor said "how many said he was nice and then there was a like a personality change…"His eyes changed, he snapped, from charming to frightening to nasty," Karmy-Jones KC said.She added that the complainant's evidence had been that "he didn't listen when I said no, he didn't stop, he didn't care, pulling pushing… thrusting"."In the rape cases, he kept on going until he achieved his ultimate aim."The prosecutor also dismissed the idea that a documentary had caused the women to "re-invent" what actually happened."There is no magic force in this documentary", she added."What in fact happened was these women have realised they are not alone and have bravely come before you to tell the truth."She added: "Truth they have lived with, which in some cases has haunted them for years."She told the jury: "The experience of people raped may be something that looms a little bit larger in your mind rather than the intricacies of the outfit."The defendant couldn't really remember anything when he was interviewed, in stark contrast to now when he suddenly seems to remember all sorts of details about the week."Addressing Brand's presented change in character, Karmy-Jones KC told the court "He may now be a completely different person to the man he was between 1999 and 2009."She added: "He may well look back and not find some of his jokes funny"."He may now treat women with kindness and consent".Brand's wife Laura gave evidence yesterday, when she told the court her husband was a "kind and a wonderful father".Karmy-Jones KC called her Russell Brand's "undoubtedly lovely wife", who "bravely" gave evidence.However, she also noted that she was not with him at the time many of the alleged acts are said to have taken place."The reality is she wasn't there then, for the first five counts, she wasn't with him, nor was she with him for the final two counts.""Any contact was, I believe, sparse."In the final set of agreed facts in his trial, the court heard from Dyer about Brand's fine after he "pleaded guilty to one charge of possessing cannabis on 20 April 1995"."He received a fine. He has no other convictions, cautions, reprimands or warnings", she said.The trial continues.

schema.headline: Russell Brand accusers 'haunted' for years by alleged crimes, court hears

title: Crypto giant Binance attempting to recover $6.3bn stolen in hack linked to North Korea
description: Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has frozen around half of the funds stolen in a "complex" hack, after $6.3bn (£4.7bn) wa
body: Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has frozen around half of the funds stolen in a "complex" hack, after $6.3bn (£4.7bn) was accessed in what is believed to be a record heist.The firm said $3bn of its stolen digital assets had been secured - but many were still in the hands of unidentified hackers. It initially thought an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing unauthorised withdrawals, but later said the attack was wider.Several analytics firms have linked the hack, which eclipses a $1.5bn (£1.12bn) heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025, to a North Korean hacking unit.The US Secret Service said it was "working around the clock" "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover" stolen funds.America's lead federal agency for investigating financial crimes added that it would "identify the cyber criminals responsible and bring them to justice", while Binance also said it was working with the FBI.The company also told its users "your money is safe, and we're covering every loss".Binance had initially suspended all deposits and withdrawals - but then said in an update that "deposits remain unaffected".Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide.The company said in 2024 that it had more than $160bn in assets under its custody.A lot of the fear right now from Binance users - and the crypto industry at large - is whether or not Binance will actually be capable of covering this enormous financial loss.The company has said repeatedly that customer funds will be covered and that the firm is strong enough to weather the storm.But crypto history watchers have been pointing out online that this is exactly the kind of message that FTX CEO Sam Bankman-Fried gave before his crypto exchange collapsed in 2022, leading to huge losses for customers and the industry.Binance has been subject of regulatory scrutiny around the world.Meanwhile, AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said that several elements of the attack resembled earlier North Korean-linked incidents, including the Bybit hack.In the last five years the crypto industry has been beset by enormous losses from hackers.In nearly all cases investigators have blamed hackers from North Korea, pointing to the infamous Lazarus Group - also know as TraderTraitor. The names refer to clusters of cyber criminals accused of working directly for the regime.Chainalysis, a crypto analytics firm, said it had "high confidence" that a North Korean is linked to the hack.North Korea is an impoverished country with very little industry and heavy international sanctions and experts say the regime uses cyber crime as a way to bring money in.North Korea has always denied this, but the wealth of evidence from cryptocurrency flow analysis and insider interviews from defectors is compelling. It makes North Korea likely to be the only nation that uses hacking as a way to raise public funds.

schema.headline: Crypto giant Binance attempting to recover $6.3bn stolen in hack linked to North Korea

title: Canada stops using 'avalanche dogs' for rescues in Rocky Mountains, stirring outrage
description: Scott Ward can still recall the relief he saw on parents' faces when a search and rescue dog he was working with found their children safe in Canada's
body: Scott Ward can still recall the relief he saw on parents' faces when a search and rescue dog he was working with found their children safe in Canada's vast and heavily wooded Banff National Park.Another time, his canine partner led him hiking up a steep mountainside for two hours until they reached a man with a broken leg who was close to dying from hypothermia.Now 73 and retired, Ward spent 17 years as a dog handler in the wilderness of the Canadian Rocky Mountains, work he described as gratifying.Over the years, the rescue programme was cut back to just one person in the role, and Ward was shocked when he heard recently that Parks Canada will end the programme entirely as of this month. Prime Minister Mark Carney's government is making broad funding cuts to Canada's public service, and Parks Canada announced last week that hundreds of their employees will soon be laid off. The agency confirmed the news to the BBC, calling it a "difficult decision" to axe its sole dog handler position out of Banff National Park, one of the most rugged parts of Canada that welcomes more than four million visitors each year from around the world. It added it is part of its efforts to modernise its law enforcement branch, and that "search and rescue operations will continue to be delivered" through other means.Cutting this one role has stirred public outrage, with more than 5,000 people signing a petition since Tuesday to restore it. William Stevenson, the Conservative Member of Parliament for the Banff area who started the petition, says he welcomes tighter government spending, but that this cut could harm public safety. "How could they possibly make such a bad choice in where to cut?" he told the BBC.The BBC has asked Parks Canada about how much the canine search and rescue programme cost to administer. For 55 years, the government used rescue dogs in the Canadian Rocky Mountains who were trained to trace "everything", Ward said, from a small paper clip to shell casings to a human body. After avalanches, a common winter hazard in the area, they were called upon to search for trapped hikers or skiers underneath heavy mounds of snow."It saves probers hours and hours of standing shoulder to shoulder and poking in the snow, and also exposing themselves to secondary avalanche hazards," Ward said.In the summer, they helped find children who got lost, often after wandering away from their parents' campsites. "We lost a huge public safety and staff safety resource," he said. Other countries still rely on canines, often called "avalanche dogs", for mountain search and rescue, including Italy, external. The last dog in Parks Canada's programme, a German Shephard named Leroy, was retired in August. For the seven years that he was on the job, Leroy helped track 156 people, find 57 who were lost in the wilderness, and solve two murders in Banff.A new canine was trained and ready for duty before Parks Canada gave notice last week that the programme would be eliminated as part of recent C$145m ($104m; £78m) budget cuts to Parks Canada, local newspaper Rocky Mountain Outlook reported.Along with his petition, Stevenson also raised the issue in Canada's parliament during a late sitting on Thursday. In response, Ryan Turnball, a Liberal MP and the parliamentary secretary for finance, said the government is focused on reducing Canada's deficit and "ensuring public funds support growth, resilience and the well-being of Canadians".Stevenson said he will continue to push on the issue, and has asked for a sit-down meeting with Parks Canada's CEO. As for Ward, he hopes that the programme will soon be restored. He recalled a quote that was often uttered by an old park warden who trained him: "You can make an armpit smell like a lilac bush and you can put a man on the moon, but nothing can replace the nose of the avalanche dog."

schema.headline: Canada stops using 'avalanche dogs' for rescues in Rocky Mountains, stirring outrage

title: US tech stocks see sharp falls over AI cost fears
description: US stocks have continued to slide as concerns continue to intensify over the increasing costs of the artificial intelligence (AI) build out.Shares in
body: US stocks have continued to slide as concerns continue to intensify over the increasing costs of the artificial intelligence (AI) build out.Shares in Intel continued their overnight slide into early trading on Friday, falling as much as 30% after the chip maker warned of a weaker computer market even as it plans to increase spending on AI.Amazon shares fell as far as 6% before recovering after its reported earnings on Thursday evening fell short of investors' expectations.The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock exchange opened on Friday at its lowest level in more than two months, down 2.5%, as other tech stocks including Reddit and Roblox continued to fall.The losses follow the value of Google owner Alphabet plunging by more than $500bn on Thursday after it revealed its own AI summaries were affecting its core search advertising revenue.Alphabet stock continued to fall in early trading, down 1% after Thursday's massive slide.The bigger losses on Friday were elsewhere, with Intel on track to lose more than $130bn in value after its earnings update rattled investors.On Thursday, Intel's finance chief David Zinsner said the firm did not expect to bring in more cash than it spent this year, and forecast lower-than-expected revenue for its fourth quarter."Looking ahead, we see the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year," he said in the chip maker's third quarter earnings report.In the earnings call, he said the firm had significantly ramped up investment in equipment in the third quarter and expected that to be "even more significant" in the following three months.Amazon on Thursday revealed the company was also spending more cash that it was making, and that spending had increased six-fold over the span of three months.Shares in Amazon recovered slightly from the overnight fall but were still down about 1.6% in Friday trading.Reddit stock was down by 26%, after the social media platform revealed weaker-than-expected daily user figures and warned that Google's growing AI-driven search was hurting referral traffic.Stock in online game platform Roblox also fell, down by nearly 20%, as its daily active user numbers dropped.Several major tech firms have reported earnings this week, including Microsoft, and analysts said there were questions about the payout from the huge investments in AI.Chris Low, from investment management firm FHN Financial, said the bulk of what was happening in the stock market was in reaction to some of the biggest tech players such as Amazon and Google.He told Reuters the companies were "showing some pretty significant growing pains as they aggressively pursue the AI build-out"."The thinking is that these signs suggest that the entire sector is going to slow down."

schema.headline: US tech stocks see sharp falls over AI cost fears

title: 'No nation left behind' says Burnham after meeting first ministers in Glasgow
description: Ministers and representatives at the summit discussed handing regions more powers to control employment support and funding for reindustrialisation. "
body: Ministers and representatives at the summit discussed handing regions more powers to control employment support and funding for reindustrialisation. "It's about creating those structures at a regional level and that is matter for Scotland and Wales to decide what that looks like in both countries," Burnham said. He urged the Scottish and Welsh governments to "work jointly" with the UK government on "a model of deeper devolution". In the context of reindustrialisation, Burnham added this could be more devolution of innovation funding. Swinney, ap Iorwerth and Burnham also agreed during the meeting there are too many young people out of work in the nations.The prime minister said the UK government would look at "arrangements for further devolution of employment support for young people in both Scotland and Wales".Devolution has been at the heart of Burnham's policy agenda since he took his place in Downing Street this summer.He claims "rewiring the state" and handing more control to regional mayors and authorities across England will boost economic growth. The prime minister's devolution at the national level has so far been less clear but Burnham has said he will listen to the administrations' calls for further powers while advocating that they share more responsibilities with local authorities. John Swinney said while he and Burnham disagree on independence, the meeting was "a welcome start" on further devolution."When the people of Scotland take issues into their own hands, the best outcomes will about," Scotland's first minister said. "To that end, I will work constructively and collaboratively with the prime minister to devolve more powers from Westminster to Scotland - as long as those proposals drive economic growth that is felt in higher wages, better jobs, more opportunities for business to start and expand, and support with the cost of living."A Downing Street spokesperson said the UK government would review issues raised by the first minister but this would not include a second independence referendum in Scotland.Rhun ap Iowerth said: "I was pleased to meet with the prime minister in Glasgow today where I once again pressed the need for Wales and the Welsh government to have the necessary tools to better serve our communities."I also reiterated the point that further devolution within Wales is a matter for the Senedd and only the Senedd."He added he welcomed the prime minister's "step forward" on the Welsh government's fiscal and borrowing powers and gave his "full support" in pushing for a stronger relationship with the EU.The prime minister had "positive discussions" with the Welsh leader, Downing Street said.A spokesperson added: "The first minister of Wales agreed to start a process to explore how each government could contribute to regional empowerment, reindustrialisation and achieving good growth in every postcode."

schema.headline: 'No nation left behind' says Burnham after meeting first ministers in Glasgow

title: US inmate Christa Pike says she woke up 'confused and in pain' after failed execution
description: Tennessee Governor Bill Lee paused all executions for the remainder of the year and ordered an independent review to "determine exactly what occurred"
body: Tennessee Governor Bill Lee paused all executions for the remainder of the year and ordered an independent review to "determine exactly what occurred".Lee was asked by reporters this week about a potential second execution attempt. "I suspect her sentence will be the same as before unless determined otherwise by the courts," he responded.Speaking about the state's response to what happened to Pike, Mann said: "I find it deeply troubling that, even after what Christa endured, Governor Lee has shown little public willingness to reconsider the death penalty itself, rather than simply the procedures used to carry it out."She added: "What happened to Christa is not an isolated tragedy, nor should this conversation begin and end with her."The Tennessee Department of Correction has not explained why the execution did not go as planned, though it has defended the method it used. It declined comment on Pike's statement when contacted by the BBC.Slemmer's mother, May Martinez, was among those pushing for Pike to be put to death and attended the botched execution, later calling it a "mess". She told a local ABC News affiliate in Florida, where she lives, that she thinks the state owes her an apology."All I wanted was justice," Martinez said. Pike was the first woman scheduled to be executed in the state of Tennessee in over 200 years.Her lawyers have spent decades appealing her case. In the days leading up to her scheduled execution, both the US Supreme Court and Lee declined to block the execution.The attempted execution of Pike was not the first in Tennessee in 2026 that did not go to plan.The execution of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and murdering three people in 1994, was postponed in May after staff were unable to find a vein for a lethal injection. He was granted a year's reprieve by the governor.In 2022, more than a third of executions across the US were botched or highly problematic, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, which does not take an ethical stance on the penalty.

schema.headline: US inmate Christa Pike says she woke up 'confused and in pain' after failed execution

title: Police watchdog to investigate Met over letter about Meghan's father
description: The UK police watchdog is to investigate the Metropolitan Police's handling of a letter containing allegations against Thomas Markle that was handed t
body: The UK police watchdog is to investigate the Metropolitan Police's handling of a letter containing allegations against Thomas Markle that was handed to his daughter, the Duchess of Sussex, in 2019.The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said it had decided an investigation was required into the force's "failure to pass on allegations of serious offending... to relevant overseas authorities at the time".The letter, written by Markle's first wife Roslyn Loveless, is believed to have contained claims about Meghan's father. He has strongly denied recent allegations that he had possessed images of child abuse, describing them as "sick lies".On Thursday the Met said it had voluntarily referred itself to the IOPC.The letter at the heart of the IOPC investigation was sent to the Met's royal protection team by Loveless, who divorced Thomas Markle in 1975 and died in 2024.The handwritten letter was then passed to Meghan in January 2019, with the duchess saying last week that it had "made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father".Meghan did not provide any details but said it had given her sufficient reason to not visit Thomas Markle and not allow him to meet his grandchildren, Archie and Lilibet.Scotland Yard said the letter contained claims about offending outside the UK and that it had been forwarded to "the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness".The IOPC will consider why the Met did not share the contents of the letter with other law enforcement agencies, in the UK or overseas.The policing watchdog also said it had decided a further matter, relating to an alleged data breach in which information was passed on to a third party, "should be returned to the force to be appropriately dealt with". No details were provided about the circumstances of the alleged breach.The Met said on Thursday that it intended to make further referrals to "relevant overseas law enforcement agencies", a process which it expected to be completed "in the coming days".The letter was forwarded by officers to the Sussexes' royal office rather than to Meghan personally, while there have been reports that the Met did not keep a copy of the letter and had to ask for one from the Sussexes.The watchdog will have to consider how the contents of the letter were treated by the force at the time.Noel Rasmussen, Thomas Markle's granddaughter and niece of the Duchess of Sussex, previously told the BBC she was "deeply troubled by the questions surrounding the Metropolitan Police's handling of the information it received". "If allegations of this seriousness were brought to the attention of authorities, it is reasonable to ask what steps were taken [and] why the information was not shared with other law enforcement agencies."Reports of the Met's handling of the letter emerged as Thomas Markle's son had told the police in the Philippines about material which was alleged to contain sexual images of children, which he had claimed to have found in possessions belonging to Meghan's father.Thomas Markle had been in the Philippines in December 2025, undergoing hospital treatment, when Meghan wrote to him to end all contact.Authorities in the Philippines have begun investigating the claims. Police there have obtained a warrant to examine devices seized from Markle's former home.Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old videotapes were handed to police by Meghan's half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, last week. However, officers in Cebu needed a court warrant before they can examine the items.Thomas Markle Sr has strongly denied all the allegations against him. He has been backed by his daughter Samantha, who has dismissed the claims against her father as "fake".

schema.headline: Police watchdog to investigate Met over letter about Meghan's father

title: Mikel Arteta warns Max Dowman 'we are not in Disneyland' after red card against Fleetwood
description: Arteta revealed that he had spoken to Dowman on Thursday and said there were "no issues at all" between the pair. However, he added that he needs to b
body: Arteta revealed that he had spoken to Dowman on Thursday and said there were "no issues at all" between the pair. However, he added that he needs to be "very straight" with Dowman and clear of the standards expected.Dowman was sent off for the England U19s earlier this month where he was also on the end of heavy challenges in a match with the United States.Of that red card, Arteta said: "They are his age. They are 16 – the same. What is the reaction? That is the level and that is the reaction."And whether it is right or wrong, that is the reaction."Arteta also spoke of the impact the red card had on the team, saying: "And the reaction when I don't win, you want to know what my reaction is? I am [angry] big time."So, we need to be ready for that. This is the environment and this is the reality, otherwise we are in Disneyland. We are not in Disneyland, we are in the Premier League and this level."We look after him so much that you cannot imagine."But at the same time we are going to demand from him, like everybody else, because he needs to earn the right to play. Because the other boys, what are they going to tell me? You need to be fair."The Gunners did appeal against the red card but the Football Association (FA) upheld the decision. Of that, Arteta said he was "very disappointed", adding "we are lucky today that he (Dowman) hasn't had a broken foot."

schema.headline: Mikel Arteta warns Max Dowman 'we are not in Disneyland' after red card against Fleetwood

title: Oleshky ceasefire: Hundreds evacuated from Russian-occupied town in Ukraine
description: A ceasefire - the longest and most widespread since the start of Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 - has been in force in the entire frontline regi
body: A ceasefire - the longest and most widespread since the start of Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 - has been in force in the entire frontline region of Kherson since Tuesday, allowing for the road out of Oleshky to be demined.Residents who wished to leave had a four-hour window to do so on Friday. A convoy of 25 buses was brought in to allow up to 750 people to leave the town until 14:00 (12:00 GMT), along with ambulances for people with limited mobility.Several hundred people are understood to have decided to stay, despite the widespread devastation and the lack of gas, electricity and running water."Everyone who wishes to leave Oleshky will be given the opportunity to do so safely," Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said on Friday morning."At the same time, those who decide to remain will be able to stay and will receive all the necessary humanitarian assistance."Ukrainian military positions lie 5km (3.1miles) from Oleshky, but the evacuees will first have to travel into Russian-occupied territory and then to the southern Russian city of Anapa. They will board a Russian government plane to Gomel in Belarus, and then drive across the border into Ukraine's Chernihiv region.Others are expected to choose to stay in Russian-occupied territory.Both Lubinets and Lantratova posted videos from Oleshky on their social media channels, saying people were given the chance to form two groups depending on whether they wanted to be taken to Russian-controlled territory or to Ukraine.In one video, Lubinets can be seen meeting tearful locals. "The problem is that a lot of people are staying," he can be heard saying. "I was told that it was their own choice, we will do everything possible for the humanitarian aid to arrive."Russia said on Thursday that it had prepared "dozens of tonnes" of aid for the residents who do not wish to leave, including food, medicine, hygiene products and fuel for generators.An Oleshky resident told the BBC she had decided against leaving because "they wouldn't take my animals, so that's it."Olena, who now lives in Kyiv, said her grandmother and wider family in Oleshky were also staying behind."The older generation does not want to leave," she told the BBC. "I've barely managed to persuade my father - and only because I've just had a baby, who he would never see otherwise." Olena's grandmother's sister died in Oleshky last winter. "She lost her legs after stepping on a landmine, covered in snow... People took her to the hospital in a garden wheelbarrow," Olena said."That's how locals transport all wounded and dead people in Oleshky to the hospital and the hospital's morgue: in garden wheelbarrows."

schema.headline: Oleshky ceasefire: Hundreds evacuated from Russian-occupied town in Ukraine

title: Syrians grow frustrated as soaring living costs threaten recovery
description: Last month, protests erupted in squares and streets across Syria. People burned tyres, blocked roads and chanted slogans, angry at the government's de
body: Last month, protests erupted in squares and streets across Syria. People burned tyres, blocked roads and chanted slogans, angry at the government's decision to raise fuel prices again. It was the largest show of discontent yet since President Ahmed al-Sharaa came to power two years ago. Speaking on a Syrian TV channel, a man said he still supported the authorities but that his situation had deteriorated to the point where he could no longer afford to buy bread. "Honestly," another said, "we have begun to fear what kind of new decision each morning will bring".The increase was the latest in a series of measures people blame for a growing cost-of-living crisis. For many Syrians, life, financially, has worsened since rebels led by Sharaa ousted President Bashar al-Assad, ending five decades of his family's brutal rule and more than 13 years of a devastating civil war. Catapulted to the presidency, Sharaa has, since then, led Syria's transition and efforts to revive a broken economy after a long period of mismanagement, isolation and conflict.There was never any doubt about how challenging this would be. But as they celebrated Assad's overthrow and their new freedoms, Syrians, perhaps unrealistically, hoped things would quickly improve. That, however, has not materialised, and the handling of the economy has frustrated many here.From essential bills to basic items, the cost of virtually everything has gone up. And many saw a further and unexpected rise in fuel prices as a sign of a government out of touch with its country. "We don't want roundabouts. Every day they build a new roundabout. People stood by you and are still with you," another protester said, addressing Sharaa, "but this will [make] things explode".Days later, amid calls for further demonstrations, the increase was revoked.In a suburb of Damascus, I joined Fatima Saleh Eid at an open-air market for her weekly shop. At 50, she works as a cleaner to help support her family. "We've suffered a lot," she said. Her husband had recently been hired by a ceramic factory after a year unemployed. He is among the lucky ones, as many are struggling to find work. In some streets, men gather in the hope of meeting someone offering a day job; often, they wait in vain.Since coming to power, the government has slashed long-held subsidies as part of an austerity drive. The price of bread, a Syrian staple, has increased tenfold. Fuel prices are now in line with the international average, which has put pressure on farmers and made transportation more expensive, while the cost of electricity has gone up several hundred per cent for some. The authorities, in response, have adjusted public sector wages, including pensions; unsurprisingly, the effect of the additional pay for people has been lost as prices keep rising."We eat more sparingly now. We can't afford chicken anymore nor meat. We only eat vegetables but even [that is] expensive," Fatima said. "Inshallah [God willing] things will get cheaper."As she spoke, around a dozen people, of all ages, gathered around us. Nobody disagreed. One elderly man also said he had stopped eating meat. Another, in his 20s, told me his family were no longer able to pay the medicine for his father, who had a heart condition. One young woman said she and her four children could only afford to have a proper meal every two days.Marwan Bashour, a 68-year-old pensioner, said his monthly pay was around $90 (£70), which is the public sector minimum wage. "It's not enough at all," he said. The United Nations Development Programme said 90% of Syrians were in poverty last year. Marwan told me how he made ends meet. "Sometimes I borrow money, sometimes I sell things from my house," he said, "like an old pot or plates that we never used, gifts that were given to us. I've even had to sell furniture".There have been other pressures too. Like many Syrians, Marwan used to rely on help from aid agencies. But, for him, that has stopped, as organisations have been forced to cut back services because of funding cuts. Syria has also not been immune to the impact of the US-Iran war. The government said the fuel increase that led to the protests was, in part, due to the pressure on energy markets because of the conflict.Sharaa has, of course, scored some important gains. International sanctions imposed in the Assad-era have been lifted, and the US has removed the country from its list of state sponsors of terrorism. Security remains volatile and a source of concern, but the country feels more stable. And the president continues to consolidate his power and, earlier this year, retook the resource-rich north-east from a Kurdish-led militia. (The Druze still control areas in the south, where they want to create an autonomous state; Israel occupies parts of the south-west.)But real economic recovery is yet to happen. Large parts of Syria remain in ruins after a war that killed half a million people and displaced half of the population. Unable to afford rent, many families live in partially destroyed buildings. The World Bank says reconstruction costs are estimated at $216bn and, without foreign help and investment, it will be impossible for Syrians to rebuild.Samir Aita, a Syrian economist who heads the Circle of Arab Economists, a Paris-based independent think-tank, said the crisis was a "combination of policies with the [government] not managing expectations and creating unrealistic hopes". When I asked him about how he felt about the future, he said: "It's unsustainable. If they don't change, I fear chaos."Exhausted after years of conflict, Syrians, left with almost no choice, remain hopeful. Abu Mahmoud, a cab driver, told me: "They inherited the country bankrupt, so people need to be patient. Things don't happen overnight."Additional reporting by Lana Antaki, Samantha Granville and Neha Sharma

schema.headline: Syrians grow frustrated as soaring living costs threaten recovery

title: 'Respected and beloved': Tributes pour in for Sir Patrick Stewart
description: Dame Judi Dench said she was "shocked" and "very sad" to hear of Sir Patrick's death, adding: "He's never been one of those actors who never felt like
body: Dame Judi Dench said she was "shocked" and "very sad" to hear of Sir Patrick's death, adding: "He's never been one of those actors who never felt like it that night, he was always very, very committed... He'll be much missed and he was much admired."George Takei, who played Hikaru Sulu in Star Trek, said the actor "inspired a whole next generation of star-gazers who looked longingly ahead to a brighter future for all humanity".Sir Patrick would later be celebrated for his portrayal of Professor Charles Xavier - most commonly known as Professor X - in the X-Men film franchise.Hugh Jackman, who starred alongside him in the franchise, called him a "tremendous friend and man", saying: "We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today."Sir Ian, a longtime friend of his X-Men co-star, who officiated his wedding in 2013, said Sir Patrick was "defined by being born and bred in Yorkshire"."You could hear it in his accented voice and in the stern honesty with which he told you what he thought and felt. Yorkshiremen have no truck with half-truths or avoidance of big issues."Sir Ian recalled first meeting Sir Patrick as young actors in the Royal Shakespeare Company (RSC) and how he had expressed caution over him taking on the Star Trek role."He took the risk and thank goodness for us all that he did," said Sir Ian, who appeared with Sir Patrick in a 2009 theatre production of Waiting for Godot.He added that while the US had become Sir Patrick's "adopted home", he "never forsook his origins" growing up in Yorkshire, and said "the proudest achievement of the most respected and beloved actor of his generation on either side of the Atlantic, was his appointment as chancellor of Huddersfield University".Sir Ian noted that Sir Patrick's final film appearance will be as Professor X in the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday film. Marvel Studios described him as "a singular talent, a generous collaborator and a true gentleman".The Academy dubbed his voice "unmistakable", adding: "Whether commanding the bridge of the Enterprise or guiding a generation of young mutants, Sir Patrick Stewart brought a tenderness to his characters that made us feel we knew them."Sir Patrick died on Wednesday "in the loving care of his wife", a statement from his family said. "We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace," it added.The veteran actor is survived by his wife, Sunny Ozell, as well as by his two adult children from his first marriage, Daniel and Sophie Stewart.Dame Harriet Walter, who first met Sir Patrick in his theatre days more than 40 years ago, said his passing was like a "huge giant tree has fallen in the forest"."He had fire in his eyes and you were absolutely in the room with him," the Succession actress told BBC Newsnight. "I've never heard a bad word against him. And I think the world's going to be very poor without him."Theatres in London's West End will dim their lights for two minutes on 3 November in his honour.  Hannah Essex, co-chief of the Society of London Theatre and UK Theatre, called him "one of the greatest stage actors this country has ever seen".As well as having roles in films such as Safe House, Robin Hood: Men in Tights and the original Dune, Sir Patrick continued to appear on TV throughout his career, making guest appearances on Frasier, Futurama and the Simpsons.US actor and animator Seth MacFarlane, who grew up as a fan of Sir Patrick, said he was "gifted the privilege of becoming a colleague and friend" as they worked together on Family Guy, American Dad! and Ted. MacFarlane described him as a "rare actor who could take any bit of dialogue and elevate it, making a good writer sound great and a great writer sound masterful".Comedian Ricky Gervais, whose BBC programme Extras Sir Patrick guest starred in, described him as a "legend".Sharing a video of the pair giggling in a set of bloopers for the series, Gervais said: "I still can't believe he agreed to do this scene. And he didn't even mind when I ruined every take."Sir Patrick was a lifelong supporter of English Football League club Huddersfield Town, which called him a "titan of his craft"."Fiercely proud of his Yorkshire roots, Sir Patrick was a Terrier in every sense, and we're proud to have counted him as one of our own," the club added.Alzheimer's is the most common type of dementia, while Lewy Body Dementia is another common form caused by abnormal protein deposits, which cause a loss of cognitive function.The Alzheimer's Society CEO Michelle Dyson said Sir Patrick was an "extraordinarily talented and much-loved actor, admired by millions around the world", adding: "His death is a heartbreaking reminder of the devastating impact dementia has on people and families across the globe."The actor became a campaigner on domestic violence in later life, including becoming an ambassador for domestic abuse charity Refuge in 2007, after witnessing his mother suffer violence at the hands of his father.Hetti Barkworth-Nanton, Refuge's board chair, said it had been a privilege to "watch his endless devotion" to the cause, adding that he "broke down barriers and taboos on the subject".Andy Burnham considered Sir Patrick to be "one of the very best" who "never forgot his working-class Yorkshire roots"."He brought joy to millions," the prime minister's spokesman said on his behalf. "He always stood up for what he believed in, including through his campaigning to help those affected by domestic violence.

schema.headline: 'Respected and beloved': Tributes pour in for Sir Patrick Stewart

title: Rugby League World Cup 2026: Set up to fail? Where England's World Cup campaign went wrong
description: As Mikey Lewis darted over for a late try in a desperate - and almost certainly fruitless - points chase against Papua New Guinea, the obituaries were
body: As Mikey Lewis darted over for a late try in a desperate - and almost certainly fruitless - points chase against Papua New Guinea, the obituaries were already being written for England's Men's Rugby League World Cup campaign.Much earlier on Friday, England's women had lacked the power and nous to overcome Samoa, losing 24-6 in a match that decided who went through to the semi-finals.England's men actually won their game - 34-12 - but it was nowhere near the margin of victory required. Their elimination will be confirmed on Sunday unless Tonga beat Samoa by more than 46 points.And so the likelihood is that for the first time in World Cup history, neither England's men nor their women will feature in the last four.For the men, that ends a run that began with Great Britain at the first tournament in 1954. The disappointment will only reinforce the idea that English rugby league needs a serious period of introspection - as well as significant investment to keep pace with the game in the southern hemisphere.But there have been other factors to trouble England at this World Cup, hosted by Australia, New Zealand and Papua New Guinea at short notice after France pulled out for financial reasons.Even before a ball was kicked, the men were faced with a sense of impending doom - brought on by injuries, shambolic travel arrangements and a bizarre format that had England facing immediate jeopardy with a testing opener against Tonga.The northern hemisphere game has deep-rooted problems, and seems to be stuck in stasis when compared with the thriving NRL. England had a record of being a major player at World Cups - having reached two finals and a further four semi-finals at the past six tournaments.But when last autumn's 3-0 Ashes series defeat by Australia prompted the departure of head coach Shaun Wane, his successor was handed a near-impossible task.Brian McDermott was appointed in April. Given just six months to prepare, the former Leeds Rhinos head coach had no mid-season international to work on a plan. Based in Australia because of his role as Gold Coast Titans assistant coach, he relied on virtual meetings to connect with his prospective squad and staff.Four on-field sessions were planned in Australia before the World Cup. But only two were completed in full after his UK-based players were subjected to a 48-hour journey to Perth that left them exhausted - a situation McDermott compared to Planes, Trains and Automobiles, the 1987 road-trip comedy starring Steve Martin and John Candy.It was a shambolic way to prepare for a pivotal opener against Tonga - one that always had the potential to consign the defeated team to an early elimination. Following that 30-12 loss, McDermott said: "You give me another two or three weeks preparation or another couple of games of preparation leading into the tournament and I'd be really excited." With the tournament organisers planning travel itineraries for the teams involved, any post-World Cup debrief ought to examine how that situation was allowed to occur. It would have made more sense for England's opener to be against France - the only other team in the men's tournament made up largely of northern hemisphere-based players.Wakefield Trinity's historic triumph may have delivered a wonderful sign-off story to the Super League season but it delivered another conundrum around England's squad selection. Had McDermott known prior to 5 October that none of the Wakefield players in his thinking would be available, could arrangements have been made for his UK-based players to travel to Australia earlier?In the end, only three of the 14 England-based players in the squad (George Williams, Matty Ashton and Ben Currie) participated in the Super League Grand Final on 3 October. "If we come together next year as a group, we will be further down the track and we don't need to start from scratch," McDermott added."Bear in mind when we landed in Perth on the Friday [9 October], we are starting... like we didn't know each other."We were putting things in place about who we are as a group, what it means to us, how we are going to play, how we are going to attack and how we are going to defend. There's been a ton of work gone on."While much of the pre-tournament noise centred on the omission of Jake Connor and England's long-running halves debate, very little focus was given to a decimated forward pack and other notable absentees. Prior the first match, McDermott recounted Australia prop Tino Fa'asuamaleaui's admiration for the strength of the English pack during last year's Ashes series. England's ability to front up had also previously been talked up by Kangaroos boss Kevin Walters.Yet McDermott had few of those same players at his disposal. Matty Lees' season-ending injury in May was not only a blow for St Helens but also robbed England of a key enforcer, one who had previously shown he could stand up to the physicality of a powerhouse Tonga front row. With second-rower Mike McMeeken and prop Caleb Hamlin-Uele unavailable, Morgan Smithies withdrawing from the squad injured and a calf complaint taking Morgan Knowles out of the equation for the encounter against Tonga, England were left short in that area. That is before you even get to options such as Sydney Roosters' Billy Smith, Wigan's Jake Wardle and Leeds Rhinos duo Ash Handley and Mikolaj Oledzki, all absent through injury.And when England had to chase the scoreboard after their defeat by Tonga - while hoping results elsewhere went in their favour - it left them in trouble. They failed to get the numbers on the board they needed against Papua New Guinea. McDermott acknowledged that it left him and his players waiting for the inevitable."It feels like we lost the game," he said. "We won and, in any circumstances I would be really proud but I think something remarkable is going to have to happen now for us to go through."We've made massive strides together in such a short period of time, in difficult circumstances where the narrative of the last two weeks is that you've got to win by 70 and 60. You don't just need to win, you need to win by massive margins."Whenever the Women's Rugby League World Cup has featured semi-finals previously, England or Great Britain have always been there. When it has not, they have always finished in the top four.But this time, they approached the tournament with a different focus, as head coach Staurt Barrow opted for youth over experience. His squad contained 11 players aged 23 or under, and was largely comprised of players who have full-time occupations away from rugby league.And that told as England were humbled 78-0 by world champions Australia last Saturday, and found wanting by a Samoa side dominated by NRL Women's Premiership talent. While Australia's domestic league pays its players, money is much tighter in England's Women's Super League."Women's Super League has progressed to a certain level and we are bringing young players through so that creeps into the national team," said Barrow. "It's good and refreshing - but at the same rate we are progressing, it's probably accelerating quicker on this side of the world if I am really honest."The investment into the NRLW is not only making the Jillaroos better but it's making all the Pacific nations better as well. "I think nearly every player for Samoa has played NRLW at some stage and that competition is improving at a rate of knots. We'll have to go back and look at what we can do in our competition."We definitely need to do something because the acceleration of the game over here is phenomenal at the moment. "Back home, we need to have more investment into the women's and girls game. It can't just be a token gesture at some clubs - and I'm not saying it is, but we need to put money into it."

title: Binance hack - who is behind it, is my money safe and what we know so far
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByLaura CressTechnology reporterBinance, the world's largest crypto exchange, has been hit by what is believed to be the lar
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByLaura CressTechnology reporterBinance, the world's largest crypto exchange, has been hit by what is believed to be the largest crypto hack ever at $6.3bn (£4.7bn).Crypto is a type of digital asset which does not exist physically like cash or coins. Instead, people use digital wallets on their smartphones or computers to access and manage it.Richard Teng, Binance's co-chief executive officer, said it is working with the authorities to work out what has happened and it will cover all losses.Here's what we know so far.What is Binance?Binance is the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange by trading volume, where people can buy, sell and trade digital currencies, like Bitcoin, as well as deposit and withdraw them.It was founded in China in 2017 and has hundreds of millions of registered users worldwide.The exchange has come under scrutiny over the past few years - notably in 2023, when its then-chief executive, Changpeng Zhao, resigned after pleading guilty to money laundering violations.Last year, a lawsuit in the US accused the company of helping send millions of dollars to US-designated terrorist organisations.In 2024, the company said it has more than $160bn in assets.How did the hack happen?The hack happened to Binance's global centralised exchange, Binance.com. Binance.us, which provides trading services specifically for US residents, said it has not been affected by the issue.In an initial announcement, Teng said: "Our initial investigation suggests this security incident may have started with a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop. "That gave an attacker access to a service container, where they submitted unauthorised withdrawal transactions."He said the hack "was not a simple 'one-click' action" but a "more complex attack process".Raghu Nandakumara, vice president of industry strategy at cybersecurity platform Illumio, said this could mean an engineer was "talked into taking a test" and malware - malicious software – "landed on their laptop while they did it".Because the laptop already had sufficient security privileges, Nandakumara said early reports suggest it became "the attacker's route straight into production, and from there to the wallets".Teng has since said the hack was "not carried out by one person" and the hackers used sophisticated methods to hide their tracks, such as a "self-destruct mechanism". "You can build a vault with mathematical firewalls, but if the individual holding the keys can be duped, the vault is opened," said Dr Clive Summerfield, head of FARx, a biometrics in AI security company.Image source, Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, Binance co-chief executive officer Richard Teng speaks at a conferenceWho is behind the hack?It is not yet known who is behind the attack, but some analytics firms have pointed to North Korea - though this has not been confirmed.AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said in a report several elements of the Binance attack resembled earlier incidents linked to the territory, including a $1.5bn (£1.1bn) hack on the ByBit exchange in 2025.These previous attacks have been linked to a cluster of cyber-criminals accused of working directly for the regime called the Lazarus Group - also known as TraderTraitor. North Korean foreign policy expert Dr Edward Howell, from the University of Oxford, has told the BBC that Pyongyang "has a long history of using cyber warfare to extract cash".Howell said North Korea "basically has a state-run cyber warfare agency", which it uses "to fund its weapons of mass destruction programmes" and as a "slush fund" for its leader Kim Jong Un's regime.Howell added that as of the current day "about 40 – 50% of North Korea's weapons of mass destruction programmes are funded by cyber and crypto-currency warfare".North Korea has always denied any involvement in these attacks; Binance has not directly responded to BBC queries about the incident's potential links to the area.What does it mean for Binance users?In his earlier statement, Teng said Binance users' funds are safe and, as a precaution, all deposits and withdrawals had been temporarily suspended.He said the firm would cover all losses from its emergency reserve set up for such situations, and make up the rest with company funds.Binance said it had been working with partners to freeze the affected assets, with around $3bn reportedly located so far. Teng said concerned users can check funds on their Binance accounts. Experts suggest doing so through the official app and website, and to reach out to the company's customer service with any questions. Users from other crypto platforms have also been warned to be wary of hackers seeking to exploit the situation.Marijus Briedis, NordVPN's chief technology officer, said people should be on the lookout for things such as "an email claiming your funds are at risk", "a fake support account offering help" or "a message urging you to move your cryptocurrency to a 'safe' wallet"."Check updates through the Binance app or a website address you already trust," he said. "Avoid links in unsolicited messages, and never give anyone your password, verification codes or wallet recovery phrase."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Binance.us said it had not been affected by the issueWhat does this mean for cryptocurrency and the wider financial system?Jennifer Craven, an international commercial fraud expert at the law firm Pinsent Masons, said the repercussions of the hack could "extend well beyond Binance"."More broadly, the incident exposes the fragility of parts of the crypto ecosystem," she said. "If a platform as sophisticated as Binance can suffer a serious attack, regulators will inevitably ask what that means for smaller, less mature platforms and currencies."She said the attack would likely accelerate scrutiny of how the sector protects both its infrastructure and its customers. Although there is no evidence yet that AI was used in this attack, it fits into a much wider concern in the financial industry of whether AI agents could potentially identify weaknesses in software and work out how to exploit them much faster than human hackers.The Bank of England has warned, external this could leave institutions struggling to fix vulnerabilities before attackers take advantage of them.How many people use cryptocurrency?Crypto has become an increasingly popular way of investing and transferring money online, partly because, unlike traditional currencies, it is not controlled by central banks or governments.This makes it popular for people who think decentralisation can bring financial freedom.But it also makes it extremely volatile, with it rising and falling in value at the whim of buyers and sellers.According to Solcard, a crypto-funded prepaid payment and virtual card platform, somewhere between 560 million and 741 million people own crypto worldwide in 2026.

schema.headline: Binance hack - who is behind it, is my money safe and what we know so far

title: Eddie Howe to Man Utd? The fans, the finances, the football structure
description: What Howe could bring to Man Utd - and what are the challenges?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Eddie Howe has been out of work since leaving
body: What Howe could bring to Man Utd - and what are the challenges?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Eddie Howe has been out of work since leaving Newcastle United in the summerBySenior football correspondentUpdated 1 hour agoWhen Sir Jim Ratcliffe became a co-owner of Manchester United in 2024, much of the narrative centred on his desire to rebuild the club around a British core.Given the expense of buying homegrown players, and the difficulties Michael Carrick -  the first permanent British managerial appointment of the Ineos era - has faced this season, perhaps Ratcliffe is rethinking.But if Carrick fails to stop the rot and loses his job, United are already considering the merits of appointing another British coach - albeit one who is more experienced.That Eddie Howe is a contender for a job that remains one of the most high-profile in world football isn't hard to fathom.Speak to those who have worked alongside Howe and they describe a man whose track record of improving players is a direct result of his relentless approach on the training field.They will also tell you Howe is someone who places an unwavering importance on the methodology of setting a winning culture.Howe may lack experience at one of the traditional top-six clubs, but his body of work at Bournemouth and Newcastle is impressive.Having been appointed Bournemouth boss with the club facing relegation from League Two in January 2009, Howe led them to the Premier League in 2015. He went on to establish the Cherries as a top-flight club before leaving - for a second time - in 2020.In 2021, Howe was appointed Newcastle manager. He led them from relegation trouble to qualification for the Champions League on two occasions and won the EFL Cup - the club's first trophy in 56 years - in 2025.Mixed reception to Howe linksOf course, managing Manchester United is an altogether different proposition.Indeed, Howe's emergence as a potential successor to Carrick has been greeted with negativity in some circles.Sections of the fanbase have been vocal on social media with their opinion that Howe isn't a big enough name to replace Carrick.Former United players Paul Scholes and Nicky Butt also fell short of providing their backing to Howe on their podcast, though it is worth pointing out they spoke in favour of the 48-year-old's potential appointment when Ruben Amorim was sacked in January.Ex-captain Roy Keane is among those to have backed Howe as a possible successor to Carrick, and other former top-flight players - including Darren Bent, Gareth Barry and Jack Wilshere - have also touted him as the man for the job.Of course, if you look hard enough you'll find voices for and against every potential manager, and it will be up to United chief executive Omar Berrada, sporting director Jason Wilcox and director of recruitment Christopher Vivell to weigh up how they proceed.Their first decision will be what happens with Carrick, and Saturday's match against Chelsea is likely to have a bearing on how United move forward.Figure caption, 'I don't need any assurances'Finances a factor in Carrick's futureIf Carrick does depart, finances will inevitably be a factor.The former Middlesbrough boss and his staff will need to be paid up before United even get to factoring in the monetary commitment towards their next head coach.While the details of Howe's agreement with Newcastle when he left in the summer remain confidential, it is understood that as things stand any club or national team would be required to pay a seven-figure compensation fee to the Magpies. Multiple sources have told BBC Sport that Newcastle - with a view to protecting themselves against Howe walking straight into another club - reached an agreement over a compensation structure that decreases over time.It is understood that figure started at £6m but has already reduced by half.The compensation payments have an expiry date - understood to be before the end of the season - at which point he can be appointed for nothing.Of course, in an industry in which astronomical figures are the norm, the prospect of paying a maximum of £3m for Howe may not be too problematic.That said, given the amount Manchester United have spent on hiring and firing managers in recent years, it is understandable if Berrada and Wilcox want to keep costs down.Would Howe fit Man Utd's footballing structure? As well as the doubts from some supporters about Howe's potential appointment, there has also been conjecture over how he would fit in United's footballing structure.At both Bournemouth and Newcastle, Howe developed a strong powerbase in all aspects of the footballing department - including recruitment.That dynamic wasn't without financial benefit to Howe's employers.The likes of Nathan Ake, Callum Wilson and Tyrone Mings were all signed by Howe at Bournemouth - and sold for a big profit by the Cherries.At Newcastle, meanwhile, Howe was instrumental in the signings of Bruno Guimarares, Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and Alexander Isak - all of whom were sold for more than they joined for. Dan Burn, Lewis Hall and Tino Livramento are among those to have developed into full England internationals under his coaching.But with a football management structure at Old Trafford that includes Berrada, Wilcox and Vivell, it is likely that Howe - at least not immediately - would not be afforded the same level of autonomy.Howe, though, is on record saying he is happy to work alongside sporting directors, and has a track record of doing so - firstly at Bournemouth under Richard Hughes, then chief executive Neill Blake.At Newcastle, he worked closely with senior management figures Dan Ashworth, Amanda Staveley and Mehrdad Ghodoussi - so fitting into Manchester United's structure wouldn't be drastically different.Whether he would want the job given the challenges, we may never know. And ultimately it is the opinion of Manchester United's decision-makers that will truly matter.'An obvious contender to replace Carrick' - analysisByChief football news reporterHowe is an obvious contender for the Manchester United job, just as he would be if the England head coach's position became available.Whether he is offered it or not will give a clear indication about the path United are going down.Director of football Jason Wilcox is thought to favour the 48-year-old, with director of recruitment Christopher Vivell preferring former Bayern Munich and Germany coach Julian Nagelsmann.Ultimately, their recommendations will be assessed by chief executive Omar Berrada, with minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe and co-chairs Joel and Avram Glazer having the final say.It is not completely clear where the negativity about Howe moving to Old Trafford comes from, other than Wilcox being targeted by Manchester United fans during the 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth. In the current managerial climate, few managers get the chance to build a body at work at one club over a number of years as, for instance, Sir Alex Ferguson did at Aberdeen before he moved south in November 1986.There is clearly a general disillusionment among the club's matchgoing fans around the football decisions taken since Ratcliffe bought his minority stake in early 2024, but Erik ten Hag, Ruben Amorim and Michael Carrick have all been backed.Some say no manager can succeed at United with the structure as it is, and it is clear whoever is in charge needs to mould together a squad bought by six permanent managers, most of whom have differing playing styles.

schema.headline: Eddie Howe to Man Utd? The fans, the finances, the football structure

title: Jack Grealish dropped by Everton: The future for ex-England winger
description: When Jack Grealish breezed back into Everton in his white Lamborghini one hour before the end of this summer's transfer deadline, the excitement among
body: When Jack Grealish breezed back into Everton in his white Lamborghini one hour before the end of this summer's transfer deadline, the excitement among supporters and the player himself was clearly evident.Grealish's previous spell on loan from Manchester City had been cut short by a serious foot injury, but the 31-year-old had produced enough moments of excitement to make his return to the Finch Farm training base a rare moment of joy amid a miserable summer in the transfer market.When Grealish finally left in the early hours - with the deal done, every autograph signed and every selfie posed for - it was a sort of homecoming for an everyman personality Everton fans had come to regard as one of their own.This was a move with a lot riding on it - for Everton manager David Moyes, who had been left with only 18 senior players after a botched transfer window, and especially for Grealish, whose exile from City at the start of the final year of his contract confirmed his banishment.Now, Grealish's future and Everton's faith in him, has reached a defining moment.Grealish's exclusion from Everton's squad before the Carabao Cup tie at home to Newcastle was publicly described as "a breach of club discipline".Specifically, it was a failure to turn up for training on Monday, leaving the talented maverick - who was Britain's first £100m footballer when he signed for City from Aston Villa in summer 2021 - facing another rebuild in his career.Everton's decision to go public before the game with the reasons for Grealish's absence emphasised the seriousness of his transgression.The fall-out means this now looks increasingly like Grealish's 'now or never' moment, because failure at Everton will surely mark a downward spiral from the top echelons of the Premier League.Everton do not regard this week's misdemeanour as marking the proverbial 'Last Chance Saloon' for Grealish. Moyes does not have enough players at his disposal to make rapid outcasts of potential game-changers.But it increases the pressure on the former England forward to win back the faith of fans who love his obvious enjoyment of life and the magic he has shown he can produce.Moyes will hope it is a harsh lesson learned, because Everton now have even more to play for, given Wembley has suddenly come into view in the Carabao Cup.BBC Sport believes there have been occasional time-keeping issues with Grealish in the past, but nothing on this scale from a personality regarded as a hard trainer who, in general, keeps himself in good condition.Grealish has held talks with those in authority at Everton, where it is sure to have been made crystal clear there must be no repeat, certainly not under a strict disciplinarian such as Moyes, and he must now attempt to be rehabilitated back into the squad.The inevitable decision to punish Grealish, taken at a high level within the club but with input and full support from Moyes, leaves him at the crossroads.That is especially the case because Everton gave arguably their best performance of the season to beat Newcastle United 3-1 and set up a quarter-final at League Two Fleetwood Town, conquerors of Premier League champions Arsenal in the last round.And it was done with the more dynamic style of 20-year-old Tyrique George playing on the left flank, which Grealish might have been expected to occupy.Moyes was guarded after the game and instead preferred to focus on a vital victory."You probably know I'm not going to give any details. It's a club decision and I support it. It's something I don't want to speak too much about," he said."The one thing about Everton is that they have got real good values. All the players stand behind it and accept the values, on the pitch and off the pitch, and I think the players did a good job."It is a small squad, but we are doing our best to keep challenging. We are not accepting any excuses for anything and I think the players are doing a great job. There was a humility about us."The words were not specifically aimed at Grealish, but they might as well have been from a manager who will have been bitterly disappointed and angry about his transgression.Moyes and Grealish formed a close relationship from virtually their first moment of contact in August 2025, the latter saying: "As soon as I spoke to the manager, I knew there was only one place that I wanted to go and that was Everton."And Grealish, a key figure when Manchester City won the Treble of Premier League, FA Cup and Champions League in 2023, played his part until sustaining a foot fracture that ended his season in Everton's 1-0 win at his former club Aston Villa in January.Grealish's happiness with life at Everton was illustrated when he decided against returning to City, continuing his rehabilitation at Finch Farm rather than going back to Etihad Stadium.Everton weighed up a second loan deal to bring Grealish back carefully, with his injury, finances and - to a certain extent - his character all entering the equation before Moyes decided to move again for a player who insisted Merseyside was the only place he wanted to be.Moyes was also juggling very limited options as owners The Friedkin Group appeared to back away from serious squad strengthening as they prepared to put the club up for sale.Grealish's form this season has been underwhelming, failing to score or create an assist in eight appearances - two of those at City before returning to Everton - while his tendency to slow play down is at odds with the usual tempo Moyes requires from his team.Moyes' fury will have increased because Grealish, who missed Saturday's loss at Arsenal through "illness", is part of a paper-thin squad that simply cannot carry passengers or have players ruling themselves out through needless ill-discipline.There will be frustration too, as Grealish is a hugely popular within Everton's dressing room as well as with staff in every area of the club. He has been described as "a lad with a heart of gold, kind and charming, who actually loves being here".This was illustrated when he recently made a £10,000 donation to a GoFundMe page for Everton fan Leon Skapars, 36, a father of three who has been diagnosed with cancer.The family are raising money in a search for treatment options, and Skapars' wife Crystal said: "In that moment, Jack gave our whole family something we desperately needed, hope. What he has done for our family is something we will never forget. It makes us feel incredibly emotional."Grealish also appeared to present awards at the Daily Mirror's 'Pride Of Britain' event recently, saying: "Footballers are classed as heroes - but these are the real heroes."On Friday, Manchester City boss Enzo Maresca refused to discuss Grealish's actions at Everton, but did praise his character.Maresca said: "It's not correct to talk about Jack in this moment, first of all because he is an Everton player and secondly because I don't have all the information."I still think he is a good guy and has a big heart."In April, Grealish extended his role as principal ambassador to Special Olympics Great Britain for a further three years, having first joined in 2022.Grealish marked the occasion by hosting five of the 10 Special Olympics GB athletes who completed the London Marathon at Everton's Hill Dickinson Stadium, surprising the athletes with a VIP experience, a stadium tour and spending time with them pitchside.Those at Everton also regard Grealish as one of the first to engage with their community programme at Finch Farm, as well as meeting with the Everton in the Community Down Syndrome team.Grealish often talks about the inspiration he takes from his sister Hollie, who has cerebral palsy.He has, however, hit the headlines in less welcome circumstances over the years, and this latest incident ushered in more.In April, Grealish was pictured asleep at a Manchester rooftop bar surrounded by drinks. It was a scene that is certainly not against the law but was at best unwise, especially with ever-present phone cameras around and the fact he was in rehabilitation from injury.In March 2020, he was fined by his club Aston Villa and apologised publicly after breaking lockdown guidelines during the pandemic after leaving his house to visit a friend.In November 2020, he admitted two counts of careless driving relating to two incidents in which a Citroen van and a Mercedes were damaged.And yet, speak to most people in football - certainly at Everton - and the character references are unfailingly glowing about his outgoing personality and kind-hearted gestures, making his breach of discipline even more painful for his many admirers.But after this latest setback, Grealish is running out of time and opportunities to justify that continued support.
